June 15, 2026  
 
[Submitted electronically to http://www.regulations.gov]  
 
The Honorable Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.  
Secretary  
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)  
200 Independence Ave SW 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
RE: [Docket No. CMS-0062-P] Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and 
Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for 
Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid 
Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care 
Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges, 
Proposed Rule  
 
Dear Secretary Kennedy,  
 
The American Pharmacists Association (APhA) appreciates the opportunity to provide HHS 
and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) comments on the “Medicare and 
Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and 
Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care 
Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and 
CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated 
Exchanges,” proposed rule.  
 
APhA represents pharmacists, student pharmacists, and pharmacy technicians in all practice 
settings, including but not limited to community pharmacies, hospitals, long-term care facilities, 
specialty pharmacies, community health centers, physician offices, ambulatory clinics, managed 
care organizations, hospice settings, and government facilities. Our members strive to improve 
medication use, advance patient care, and enhance public health.  
 
In January 2017, APhA joined a workgroup of 17 state and specialty medical societies, national 
provider associations, and patient representatives to develop best practices for prior 
authorization and other utilization management requirements by identifying the most common 
concerns among providers and patients. APhA recommends that CMS reference the 21 Prior 
Authorization and Utilization Management Reform Principles in the workgroup’s report, which 
2 
 
address clinical validity; continuity of care; transparency and fairness; timely access and 
administrative efficiency; and alternatives and exemptions. Many CMS proposals align with 
these principles, and APhA encourages CMS to ensure final policies align with them to ensure 
that implementation achieves the intended reductions in administrative burden and 
improvements in patient access. 
 
Pharmacists and pharmacy technicians spend countless hours navigating prior authorization 
requests and requirements, taking away time that could be spent on patient care services or on 
preparing and dispensing medications. Patients also feel the impact of the prior authorization 
process, as this process often causes delays in treatment and leads patients to forgo getting the 
prescribed medications. Because pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, and other pharmacy 
personnel are the ones having to explain this process to patients at the pharmacy counter, 
patients can become frustrated with pharmacists and pharmacy staff because the coverage rules 
are confusing, and the processes for submitting requests can be cumbersome, sometimes relying 
on responses sent via fax machines. Due to this negative impact on both pharmacy operations 
and patient access, APhA opposes prior authorization programs that create barriers to patient 
care or impose unfunded mandates on our nation’s pharmacists who are not insurance issuers. 
APhA urges CMS, as part of this rule, to simplify the prior authorization process and make 
prior authorization conditions and requirements more accessible to health care providers, 
including pharmacists and pharmacy technicians, so that they can spend less time on prior 
authorizations and more time on patient care. APhA further urges CMS to ensure that prior 
authorization reforms include real-time, patient-specific formulary and benefit information at 
the point of prescribing and dispensing, including clear indicators of prior authorization, step 
therapy, and cost-sharing requirements. These capabilities would reduce claim rejections at the 
pharmacy counter and improve timely access to medications. This approach aligns with CMS’s 
proposal to require the use of NCPDP Formulary & Benefit (NCPDP F&B) and Real-Time 
Prescription Benefit (NCPDP RTPB) standards, as well as with established utilization 
management reform principles calling for transparent, up-to-date, and patient-specific coverage 
information to support provider decision-making. 
 
In the proposed rule, CMS notes that in previous comments related to the topic, commenters 
recommended they “reconsider the exclusion of drugs from [their] proposals and suggested 
that CMS finalize the prior authorization process and Prior Authorization API [Application 
Programming Interfaces] requirements in the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization final rule to cover drugs covered under a medical benefit” and “expressed that 
by failing to include drugs in those requirements, CMS was failing to address the biggest culprit 
of delay to timely care and administrative burden.”1 CMS is now “proposing to require that 
impacted payers support electronic prior authorization for all drugs that require prior 
 
1 Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed 
Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP 
Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges, 91 
Fed. Reg. 19890, 19892 (Apr. 14, 2026). Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-57.  
3 
 
authorization.”2 To do so, CMS is “proposing two separate sets of standards to facilitate 
electronic prior authorization for all drugs, the HL7 FHIR standard (and certain FHIR IGs) as 
one set, and three NCPDP standards (the NCPDP SCRIPT standard, NCPDP Formulary & 
Benefit Standard Implementation Guide, and the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit 
Standard Implementation Guide) as the other set.”3 The rule goes on to outline that “[t]he FHIR 
standard, including the IGs, and the three NCPDP standards, all facilitate electronic prior 
authorization for drugs; which standards set is applicable depends on whether the drug is 
covered under the payer's medical benefit or its pharmacy benefit.”4 The Prior Authorization 
API, which comprises the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery IG, the HL7 
FHIR Da Vinci Documentation Templates and Rules IG, and the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci Prior 
Authorization Support IG, should only be used for drugs under a medical benefit.5 While the 
NCPDP SCRIPT standards should be used for drugs under the pharmacy benefit.6 CMS 
explains in the proposed rule that “these sets of FHIR and NCPDP standards are mutually 
exclusive and, when used in conjunction, encompass the full scope of drugs that are covered by 
any particular payer.”7 
 
NCPDP Standards for Prior Authorization of Drugs Covered Under a Pharmacy Benefit (FR 19901) 
 
As noted above, CMS is “proposing to require impacted payers to use either the FHIR 
standards and IGs required for the Prior Authorization API or the NCPDP SCRIPT standard 
depending upon whether the drugs are covered under a medical benefit or a pharmacy 
benefit.”8 APhA supports the use of these standards to streamline the prior authorization 
process, reducing barriers to patient care and saving pharmacists and pharmacy technicians 
time in managing these requests. This proposal is directly aligned with widely recognized best 
practices that call for prior authorization processes to be conducted exclusively through 
standardized electronic transactions rather than fax, telephone, or proprietary web portals. 
Standardization across payers, as proposed by CMS, reflects long-standing recommendations to 
reduce administrative complexity and improve efficiency for pharmacies, which otherwise must 
navigate widely varying requirements across plans. 
 
As discussed in the proposed rule, NCPDP “is responsible for developing and maintaining 
standards for the exchange of information between providers, pharmacies, and payers[,]”9 and 
“the NCPDP SCRIPT standard is the most widely used standard by providers and payers for 
electronic prescribing and electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under a pharmacy

benefit.”10 As summarized by CMS, NCPDP SCRIPT “can support a complete workflow around 
determining whether prior authorization is required” when used with NCPDP F&B or NCPDP 
RTPB standards, to “facilitate a three-way transaction to notify providers and pharmacies when 
prior authorization has been requested[,]” “support both the workflow to determine whether 
prior authorization is required and the coverage and documentation requirements to receive a 
decision, as well as the technical processes to send prior authorization requests from a provider 
to a payer, followed by the payer’s responses (for example, approved, denied, and additional 
information required)[,]” “minimize manual data entry by the provider based on information in 
the EHR or other health IT system[,]”11 and “send information to a payer (or the payer’s PBM) 
in real time, which should result in faster prior authorization approvals and therefore faster 
patient access to medications compared to manual prior authorization processes.”12 By 
simplifying the prior authorization process in this manner, the time spent reviewing and 
responding to payer documentation requirements should be reduced, giving patients answers 
sooner and lessening the burden the prior authorization process places on pharmacists and 
pharmacy technicians.  
 
Additionally, the proposed rule notes that if finalized, “impacted payers could use an 
unexpired version of the NCPDP F&B standard adopted by the Secretary to provide a range of 
formulary and benefit information, such as formulary status, preferred alternatives, benefit 
coverage, and estimated co-pay information to end users, including providers, at the time of 
prescribing.”13 Providing this level of information at the point of prescribing should help to 
reduce the number of prior authorizations, saving those assisting patients in this process, 
including pharmacists and pharmacy technicians, time and resources, and allowing patients to 
access their needed medications more quickly. Furthermore, if finalized, CMS would require 
the NCPDP RTPB standard, which “enables the real-time exchange of patient-specific eligibility, 
drug coverage (including any restrictions and alternatives), and estimated cost sharing to 
enable access to this information at the point of prescribing.”14 As the proposed rule states, 
“[t]he NCPDP F&B and NCPDP RTPB standards can complement each other in the provider’s 
workflow to allow for relevant formulary, coverage, cost, and prior authorization information 
to be utilized when prescribing a drug,” giving providers “a more complete view of patient-
specific medication options, costs, and prior authorization information at the point of 
prescribing.”15 Because these standards should reduce the workload associated with the prior 
authorization process and enable patients to obtain their prescribed medications more quickly, 
APhA supports the use of the NCPDP standards outlined in the proposed rule. 
 
In addition, APhA encourages CMS to incorporate explicit continuity-of-care protections into 
prior authorization policies. Patients whose conditions are stable on existing therapies should

not experience interruptions in treatment due to new prior authorization or step therapy 
requirements, particularly during coverage transitions. 
 
These protections would complement CMS’s broader efforts to streamline prior authorization 
and ensure timely access to care, consistent with best practices that call for maintaining therapy 
continuity, prior authorization approvals for the duration of treatment, and preventing 
unnecessary repetition of step therapy protocols. 
 
Proposed Requirement to Incorporate Drugs Covered Under a Medical Benefit Into the Prior 
Authorization API For All Impacted Payers (FR 19923) 
 
CMS is “proposing to require impacted payers to expand the scope of the required Prior 
Authorization API to incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit.”16 CMS reasons, “that 
enhancing the Prior Authorization API by incorporating drugs covered under a medical benefit 
would improve the prior authorization process by giving providers and patients more timely 
information about prior authorization requirements to obtain these drugs.”17 Additionally, the 
proposed rule states that including “drugs covered under a medical benefit would streamline 
the administrative process for providers and result in payers receiving more complete requests 
and fewer unnecessary requests, which could accelerate decision-making.”18 CMS notes that 
“adding drugs covered under a medical benefit to the non-drug items and services included in 
the Prior Authorization API requires no changes to the existing standards.”19 As such, APhA 
supports CMS in implementing these standards and requirements to streamline the prior 
authorization process and reduce associated barriers to patient care.  
 
Improving Communication and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations (FR 19932) 
 
CMS notes in the proposed rule that lengthy wait times for prior authorization decisions 
negatively affect patient care and burden providers.20 To combat this, the proposed rule builds 
upon CMS’s previous work by requiring impacted payers to provide a specific reason for denial 
when responding to providers for non-drug items and services, and by adding the same 
requirement for denied prior authorizations for all impacted payers under this rule.21 CMS 
reasons that “[w]hen a payer provides a specific reason for a denial, a provider can take 
appropriate actions such as resubmitting the request with updated information, appealing the 
decision, or identifying alternative drugs or treatments.”22 APhA supports such regulations 
because they give providers, including pharmacists, greater access to coverage information, 
enabling them to respond to these denials more effectively. APhA further notes that CMS’s

18 Id.

proposal to require specific reasons for prior authorization denials is strongly aligned with best 
practices emphasizing transparency and clinical clarity in utilization management decisions. 
Denial explanations should include a clear clinical rationale, identification of missing 
information, and any covered alternatives, enabling pharmacists and other providers to take 
timely and appropriate next steps. 
 
Enhancing denial transparency, as proposed by CMS, will reduce unnecessary resubmissions 
and delays in therapy and improve pharmacists’ ability to coordinate care at the point of 
dispensing. 
 
The proposed rule also outlines prior authorization decision timeframes for different types of 
plans, issuers, and entities. CMS proposes that qualified health plan issuers on the federally-
facilitated exchanges “must notify a requesting provider of their decision as expeditiously as the 
enrollee’s health condition requires, but no later than 72 hours after receiving a standard prior 
authorization request and no later than 24 hours after receiving an expedited prior 
authorization request.”23 The proposed rule notes that this timeframe aligns “with current and 
proposed timelines for other impacted payers, could improve patient care and minimize 
administrative burden for providers who would be able to expect prior authorization decisions 
within the same timeframe from all impacted payers.”24 APhA appreciates CMS’s work to 
standardize these timelines as much as possible, given other applicable rules impacting the 
variety of impacted payers subject to this proposed rule. Because shorter timelines reduce 
barriers to patient care and increase efficiency, APhA supports CMS’s work to keep these 
timelines as short as possible.  
 
APhA notes that CMS’s proposed timelines are consistent with widely supported benchmarks 
for prior authorization decision-making and represent an important step toward improving 
responsiveness across payers. Timely determinations are especially critical in pharmacy 
settings, where delays often lead to prescription abandonment and interruptions in therapy 
initiation. 
 
Aligning timelines across payers, as proposed by CMS, will further reduce administrative 
burden and improve predictability for pharmacists and patients alike. 
 
Additionally, CMS is “proposing to require impacted payers to annually report certain metrics 
about prior authorizations for all drugs (excluding covered Part D drugs for MA-PDs) by 
posting this information on their public website.”25 More specifically, CMS “propose[s] that 
impacted payers, other than Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities, be 
required to annually report the previous calendar year’s metrics regarding all drugs, excluding 
covered Part D drugs for MA-PDs, on their public websites beginning in 2028 (with data from 
 
23 Id. at 19936. Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-520.  
24 Id. Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-522.  
25 Id. at 19941. Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-605.  
7 
 
2027) following any calendar year that any of these impacted payers offered that type of plan.”26 
APhA appreciates CMS’s efforts to ensure that information regarding prior authorizations, 
especially denials, is publicly reported to promote both accountability and transparency. 
Increased transparency will enable stakeholders to better evaluate the impact of prior 
authorization policies and identify opportunities for improvement. 
 
While APhA supports CMS’s proposals to improve prior authorization processes, APhA also 
encourages CMS to consider policies that reduce the overall volume of prior authorizations, 
such as limiting requirements to outlier prescribing patterns or adopting “gold carding” 
approaches for providers with demonstrated adherence to evidence-based prescribing. These 
approaches would build on CMS’s current proposals by further reducing unnecessary 
administrative burden across the health care system. 
 
Provider Access API (FR 19951) 
 
The proposed rule notes that CMS “in the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization 
final rule … required impacted payers to implement and maintain a FHIR API that makes 
patient data available to providers who have a contractual relationship with the payer and a 
treatment relationship with the patient.”27 In that same rule, CMS “required impacted payers, 
including individual market QHP issuers on the FFEs, to build a Payer-to-Payer API, with 
certain standards that would facilitate patient data exchange at the start of coverage and 
between concurrent payers.”28 As CMS continues to propose changes to these requirements and 
others related, APhA encourages CMS to consider providing pharmacists with access to this 
data when appropriate. Creating mechanisms to exchange patient information with pharmacists 
can accelerate the overall expansion of interoperability with pharmacists and pharmacies in the 
future, and APhA urges CMS to establish a timeline for pharmacy interoperability. Expanding 
pharmacist access to these data, consistent with CMS’s broader interoperability framework, 
would enhance care coordination, reduce duplicative administrative work, and allow more 
efficient resolution of prior authorization issues at the point of dispensing. 
 
Regarding credential verification and authentication, which is discussed throughout the 
proposed rule, Pharmacy Profiles verifies credentials for pharmacy professionals nationwide. 
As CMS works to recognize pharmacists as providers capable of submitting and receiving data, 
it should use Pharmacy Profiles as a provider directory data source for pharmacists and 
pharmacy professionals. 
 
Request for Information: Step Therapy (FR 20013)  
 
Regarding step therapy, “[a]uthorization of the non-preferred drug may require attestation by 
the provider that the patient took the initial drug and experienced adverse effects or that the 
 
26 Id. at 19942. Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-607.  
27 Id. at 19951. Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-772.  
28 Id. at 19952. Available at: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-07205/p-791.  
8 
 
initial drug provided inadequate clinical benefit.”29 The overall step therapy process, along with 
potential delays related to provider attestations, can hinder patient access to the medications 
that work for the patient, potentially leading to disease progression. Within the proposed rule, 
CMS is seeking more information on “whether increased interoperability of information 
technology (IT) systems across payers could be used to make utilization management policies, 
such as step therapy, more transparent.”30 Given the frequent touchpoints pharmacists have 
with their patients after dispensing medication, they are often the first to know if a medication 
is not working for a patient or if the patient is experiencing adverse effects. Accordingly, APhA 
encourages CMS to expand interoperability with pharmacies to allow pharmacists to provide 
input on drug therapies the patient may have tried and to submit additional information that 
other parties involved may need in real time, thereby streamlining parts of the step therapy 
process and attestations. Streamlining these processes reduces barriers in the current prior 
authorization process, enabling patients to access the medications they need more quickly.  
 
APhA further encourages CMS to ensure that step therapy policies include efficient 
mechanisms for exceptions and overrides when clinically appropriate. These recommendations 
are consistent with broader efforts to improve utilization management processes by allowing 
timely flexibility and ensuring that patients are not subject to unnecessary delays in accessing 
clinically appropriate therapies. 
 
Leveraging interoperability tools, as CMS explores in this RFI, to enable pharmacists to 
contribute real-time information on therapeutic failures or adverse effects would further 
streamline step-therapy processes and improve patient outcomes. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on this proposed rule. If you have any 
questions or would like to meet with APhA and our nation’s pharmacists, please contact Corey 
Whetzel, APhA’s Senior Manager, Regulatory Affairs, at cwhetzel@aphanet.org.  
  
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
Michael Baxter  
Vice President, Government Affairs

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Pharmacists Association (APhA); signed by Michael Baxter, Vice President, Government Affairs.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents pharmacists, student pharmacists, and pharmacy technicians across community pharmacies, hospitals, long-term care, specialty pharmacies, community health centers, physician offices, ambulatory clinics, managed care, hospice, and government settings.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

APhA supports CMS proposals to streamline drug prior authorization through NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit drugs, FHIR APIs for medical benefit drugs, denial transparency, shorter/standardized decision timeframes, and public PA metrics. APhA urges CMS to ensure reforms reduce pharmacy burden, provide real-time patient-specific benefit/formulary information, protect continuity of care, expand pharmacists' access to interoperability data, and use pharmacy input in step therapy workflows.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL/RFI Step Therapy; Provider Access API and Payer-to-Payer API related interoperability.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Federal Register page references including FR 19901, 19923, 19932, 19951, and 20013; no CFR citations emphasized.
- **Standards referenced:** NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP Formulary & Benefit; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit; HL7 FHIR; Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS; Provider Access API; Payer-to-Payer API.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB can reduce fax/phone/portal workflows, provide real-time patient-specific information, and reduce rejected claims at the pharmacy counter.
- **Specific request:** Finalize NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit ePA and ensure point-of-prescribing and point-of-dispensing access to formulary, benefit, PA, step therapy, and cost-sharing information.

**Topic 2: FHIR PA API for medical benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Adding medical benefit drugs to the existing PA API requires no changes to existing standards and can streamline provider workflow and reduce barriers.
- **Specific request:** Finalize incorporation of medical benefit drugs into the Prior Authorization API.

**Topic 3: Denial reasons and communication**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Specific denial reasons help pharmacists and other providers respond more efficiently, reduce resubmissions, and coordinate care.
- **Specific request:** Denial explanations should include clinical rationale, missing information, and covered alternatives.

**Topic 4: Decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Shorter timelines reduce prescription abandonment and therapy interruption.
- **Specific request:** Keep timelines as short and standardized as possible, including 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited QHP timeframes.

**Topic 5: PA metrics and accountability**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS / TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Public reporting improves transparency and helps stakeholders assess prior authorization impacts.
- **Specific request:** Finalize annual PA metrics reporting and consider broader burden-reduction policies such as gold carding.

**Topic 6: Pharmacist access to interoperability data**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL / Provider Access API
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Pharmacists need data to coordinate care and resolve PA issues at dispensing.
- **Specific request:** Provide pharmacists with appropriate Provider Access API data access, establish a timeline for pharmacy interoperability, and use Pharmacy Profiles as a provider directory source.

**Topic 7: Step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI S66-S82
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Pharmacists often know when a medication failed or caused adverse effects and can supply real-time information to streamline exceptions.
- **Specific request:** Expand interoperability with pharmacies for real-time pharmacist input and ensure efficient exceptions/overrides for clinically appropriate cases.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Supports incorporating medical benefit drugs into the PA API.
- **S14:** Supports NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit drug PA.
- **S16:** Supports specific denial reasons for all drug prior authorization denials.
- **S17:** Recommends denial explanations include clinical rationale, missing information, and covered alternatives; implies support for structured/actionable denial detail.
- **S20/S43:** Supports shorter, standardized decision timeframes across payers.
- **S22:** Supports NCPDP standards as burden-reducing for pharmacists and pharmacy technicians.
- **S25:** Supports RTPB use because it provides patient-specific eligibility, coverage restrictions, alternatives, and estimated cost sharing.
- **S29/S35:** Supports public reporting of PA metrics to promote accountability and transparency.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to step therapy RFI by recommending pharmacy interoperability, pharmacist input on prior therapy failures/adverse effects, and efficient exceptions.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Reference and align final policies with the 21 Prior Authorization and Utilization Management Reform Principles.
2. Finalize NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB standards for pharmacy benefit drug PA.
3. Ensure real-time, patient-specific formulary, benefit, PA, step therapy, and cost-sharing information at prescribing and dispensing.
4. Finalize expansion of the FHIR Prior Authorization API to medical benefit drugs.
5. Require specific denial explanations with clinical rationale, missing information, and covered alternatives.
6. Standardize and shorten PA decision timelines.
7. Publicly report PA metrics for transparency and accountability.
8. Consider limiting PA volume through outlier-based policies and gold carding.
9. Provide pharmacists with appropriate access to Provider Access API data and establish a pharmacy interoperability timeline.
10. Use Pharmacy Profiles as a provider directory data source for pharmacy professionals.
11. Use interoperability to streamline step therapy attestations, exceptions, and overrides.
12. Incorporate continuity-of-care protections so stable patients are not interrupted by new PA or step therapy requirements.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Pharmacy burden, treatment delays, confusing coverage rules, fax/manual processes, prescription abandonment, lack of pharmacist access to data, step therapy delays.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Patients forgo medications, frustration at pharmacy counter, therapy interruptions, disease progression, unnecessary repetition of step therapy.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Variation across payers, limited pharmacist access to interoperability infrastructure, need for credential verification and provider directory inclusion.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No original quantitative data; quotes Federal Register descriptions of NCPDP and FHIR standards and workflows.
- **Studies or research referenced:** 21 Prior Authorization and Utilization Management Reform Principles workgroup report.
- **Examples provided:** Pharmacy counter claim rejections; fax-based PA responses; pharmacist knowledge of treatment failure/adverse effects; Pharmacy Profiles credential verification.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, patients, prescribers, payers/PBMs, pharmacies, managed care organizations.
- **Economic implications:** Reduced manual PA burden could save staff time; real-time benefit information may reduce claim rejections and prescription abandonment.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports using established NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit and FHIR/Da Vinci for medical benefit; calls for pharmacy interoperability expansion.
- **Patient care impact:** Positive if reforms reduce delays, preserve continuity of therapy, improve PA transparency, and streamline step therapy exceptions.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with additional recommendations
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, provider-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "APhA supports the use of these standards to streamline the prior authorization process, reducing barriers to patient care and saving pharmacists and pharmacy technicians time." - Context: NCPDP pharmacy benefit standards.
2. "Providing this level of information at the point of prescribing should help to reduce the number of prior authorizations." - Context: NCPDP F&B support.
3. "Denial explanations should include a clear clinical rationale, identification of missing information, and any covered alternatives." - Context: Recommended denial explanation content.
4. "APhA encourages CMS to expand interoperability with pharmacies to allow pharmacists to provide input on drug therapies the patient may have tried." - Context: Step therapy RFI response.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on pharmacist and pharmacy technician time spent on PA.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Emphasizes medication delays, abandonment, and timely access.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Addresses NCPDP, FHIR, API access, and interoperability implementation.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Supports established NCPDP and FHIR/Da Vinci standards.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports denial reasons and public PA metrics.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for pharmacist inclusion in interoperability and directory workflows.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Seeks to replace fax/phone/portal processes with standardized electronic transactions.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Discusses health IT systems, EHRs, Pharmacy Profiles, and APIs.
